title: Start workflows from schedules and signed webhooks

props.description: Configure governed workflow starts from native schedules, GitHub events, and Standard Webhooks.

text.insert: Native schedules, GitHub events, and Standard Webhooks deliveries start ordinary governed workflow runs through triggers. A trigger binding selects the workflow, execution user, inputs, execution host, shared resource, and overlap policy. The schedule or webhook decides when to request a start; it does not bypass workflow validation, provider configuration, isolation, or resource admission.
Schedules and event bindings are deployment configuration. They do not belong in workflow YAML.

Choose a resource, capacity, and overlap policy

names the work that must not overlap. Use the same sufficiently qualified resource for every schedule or webhook binding that can mutate that work. A trigger ID or workflow name does not imply a resource.
sets how many runs can hold the resource at once. It is optional and defaults to
, so by default runs for one resource never overlap. Set it higher for work that tolerates a bounded number of concurrent runs, such as
. Every binding that names a resource must declare the same capacity. A start that declares a different capacity is rejected and recorded as
instead of silently using either value. To change a resource's capacity, use a new resource name.
setting controls a request that arrives while the resource is full:
records the blocking run and retains no promise to execute later.
retains the prepared request in durable FIFO order.

A queued request also blocks newer requests for the same resource, so a new arrival never passes older queued work, except work held back because another run holds its checkout (below). Different resources can run concurrently. Pending and running root runs hold their resource; a run releases it when it completes, fails, or is cancelled.

A paused run gives back its resource at a host-continued wait or gate. Once its process stops at a time or event wait, or at an approval gate or attention wait, the run releases its slot and later work can be admitted. Its continuation takes a slot again before it executes, ahead of queued new starts, because the run never lost its admission. When the resource is full, the run stays
, keeps any answer it was given, and waits for capacity:

, and a continuation host retries it about once a minute. Paused runs that wait for capacity take free slots in the order they were first refused. A refused resume keeps the run's place once it is ready to continue, its wait due or signaled or its pause answered, whichever surface resumed it. A refused resume of a run that is not ready records no place, so it holds no capacity. A parent blocked on a child workflow, a container write-back, and any container run keep their slot until they continue, because no continuation host retries them. A run paused because its source is unreadable also keeps its slot, even when a continuation host will retry it. Automatic continuation of waits, gates and unreadable-source pauses requires a continuation host:
. Runs paused before this behavior existed keep their slot until they continue.

A run admitted on a resource holds its checkout until it completes, fails, or is cancelled, including while it is paused and has given back its slot. Admission therefore passes over a queued request that would run in a checkout another run admitted on the same resource holds: the same
directory, or the same explicit worktree

in that codebase. The request keeps its place in the queue, and the free slot goes to the next request that can run. When that run ends, the request is admitted ahead of later requests for that checkout, one request per checkout at a time. A new request for a held checkout queues, or with
is skipped, with the holding run as its blocker. A worktree lane without a
gets its own checkout and is never held back this way.

Guarded starts also wait behind live runs outside the resource, including manual runs and runs on other resources, when they hold the same directory or registered reusable worktree. The holding run is named in inspection. Workflows declaring

can proceed beside these foreign holders; same-resource checkout serialization still applies. The resolved declaration is captured during preparation, so later workflow edits do not change a queued request. Older stored requests without that declaration are treated as guarded. Admission observes holders without changing their state. Foreign pending runs hold their checkout only during the executor's five-minute dispatch window; running and paused holders keep blocking until they end. Expiry releases only foreign checkout occupancy, leaving the pending run and any resource admission unchanged.
A drain processes untouched queued requests assigned to one host and admits them while the resource has free capacity.

Host listing retains failures for damaged requests assigned to the selected host, including malformed launches or a file request that disagrees with its containing slot. The host drains independent resources before reporting those failures together, preserving the request ID and original error (and the document path for file requests). On a damaged resource, drains can admit valid predecessors up to the first malformed request; they never pass that entry. Damaged data stays unchanged for repair. Direct resource drains use the same valid prefix and log the damaged request ID; new admission, resume, and request inspection remain strict.
reports failures belonging to its receipt as command failures. Failures belonging to other receipts, or whose receipt cannot be identified, produce warnings while the accepted receipt is printed;
still fails for any reported drain failure.

In the file store, a missing or corrupt slot queue or request envelope may hide which host owns a candidate. Listing reports those unclassifiable candidates as unattributed failures with their document paths and original errors. The host attempts independent resources before reporting failure. Unreadable slot membership reports its document error when it could affect admission, drain, or resume. An intact admitted request on a different resource with a provably separate checkout does not prevent independent work from draining. Repair damaged documents before relying on drain to reach their resource or checkout. A request whose host is known is reported as a failure even when it is the resource's only queued member. A start receipt that cannot be read or validated is reported on every host pass as an unattributed failure naming its document path and keeping the original error. Its bindings are not prepared until the document is repaired; the document is left unchanged, and other receipts and queued requests continue.
The server rechecks its own host about every five seconds, including requests waiting on foreign holders.

runs one drain and can run after every earlier Archon process has exited, because the queue is durable. For CLI-only hosts, schedule this drain to keep queued work advancing after a foreign holder ends. Neither recovers a request that was already admitted to a run.
A malformed stored checkout-guard declaration is never admitted. Drains pass over that request and log

with its request ID, so valid queued work can continue. The request stays queued and can be inspected and withdrawn with the trigger CLI. New starts with malformed declarations are rejected before storage.

If a known foreign admitted run has a missing or corrupt stored launch and no recorded working path, admission cannot identify its checkout. Guarded starts targeting an in-place path or explicit branch wait (or skip) with that run named as blocker until its launch is repaired or it ends; read-only starts and branchless worktrees can still proceed. SQL logs

The file store records admitted run membership in its slot independently of the request, retaining it when a paused run gives back capacity. Slot documents written by older versions remain readable; releasing an older holder records its membership before removing the capacity holder. In both stores, surviving local slot membership requires a matching admitted request; admission, drain, and other local resumes fail until that evidence is repaired or the holder ends. Recorded slot membership determines whether a holder is local or foreign, even when its request falsely names another resource. A request that disagrees with its local slot membership is rejected; a proven foreign holder still permits read-only starts.

A run released by an older version may have neither retained membership nor a capacity holder. Its request alone cannot establish its resource: a request with readable admitted status, resource, and prepared launch keeps that checkout serialized even for read-only starts, while independent checkouts can proceed. Damaged

fields do not prevent this checkout-only observation. Direct local requests and resume still require a valid complete request. Unreadable checkout projections fail admission and direct drains explicitly. An intact admitted request without contradictory slot membership can resume through normal capacity arbitration, including a paused or failed run released before the upgrade. The checkout remains held while the run is paused.

When independent slot membership is absent, a historical resume trusts the surviving structurally valid admitted request's resource association. If that resource field was damaged to name another valid resource, serialization on the original resource is not guaranteed until the admission evidence is repaired or the holder ends. Surviving contradictory membership is still rejected, guarded starts still wait behind foreign checkout holders, and capacity waiters keep their original priority.

If an older released holder also loses its request document, the stored data cannot distinguish it from a manual run. It receives foreign-holder behavior, so read-only starts can pass it even on its former resource. Preserve or repair the request and slot membership before relying on same-resource serialization in that damaged state.

POSIX host commands that started or completed also produce a warning about possible untracked background work, including after continuation. Neither a survivor nor cleanup is confirmed. These owner-stop warnings retain owned checkouts; inspect processes with

process stopped with SIGTERM or SIGINT marks its own running run failed before it exits, which also releases the resource. A crash or SIGKILL cannot do that and leaves ownership ambiguous.
If an admitted run has ambiguous ownership after a crash, inspect the request and its blocking run.

is the explicit escape hatch here. If the run's owner answers on this host, abandon stops its safely targetable process groups before recording the run cancelled. A waiting start can then be admitted, even if an output-holder warning reports that an unsignalled process still holds node output. Abandon retains owned checkouts when owner-stop warnings report held output or possible untracked background work, including descendant checkouts and their root. Use

on the retained checkout before reusing or removing it. If no owner answers, abandon records the run cancelled and prints the host and pid the run recorded; an owner on another host cannot be stopped from here, so verify it has stopped before abandoning. Archon does not abandon a run because it is old or unreachable. Automatic queue draining and recovery of ambiguous execution are separate operations.

The maintained GitHub source plugin supports issue and pull-request lifecycle events, issue or pull-request label changes, comments created on an issue or pull request (
event), check-run changes, and commit-status changes. A label change carries who made it, as the

; the comment's text is not part of the event. Selectors match an exact event kind and one of the configured actions. They can also restrict the repository, issue or pull-request number, and the predicates supported for that event kind. Input mappings copy a supported event field or supply a typed JSON literal. A required field that is unavailable rejects that binding instead of inventing a value.

The plugin authenticates the raw payload using the configured shared secret. The server validates its resolved receipt, verifies for a new delivery that the configured run-as users exist, and commits the receipt before returning success. Preparing and starting the run happen after the response, so a slow workflow never delays GitHub's delivery. An invalid signature creates no trusted receipt. A signed source event does not select the Archon user who runs the workflow. Every binding must name an authorized
. The optional GitHub event actor remains provenance and never becomes an Archon credential selector.
On the first verified delivery, Archon records the source instance, delivery ID, verified-content digest, selected binding ID and revision, resolved inputs, and launch intent. Replaying the same

reuses the original receipt and binding snapshot; changed or newly added bindings do not create starts for that delivery. Editing a binding does not turn an old delivery into a new start. Reusing a delivery ID with different verified content returns HTTP 409. When GitHub supplies no delivery ID, Archon cannot provide source-level replay deduplication.

GitHub does not automatically redeliver every failed webhook. Check delivery status in GitHub and use GitHub's explicit redelivery or your reconciliation process after a transport or processing failure. Archon retains safe receipt and disposition data for inspection; it does not retain the raw webhook body as a trigger archive.

Sign a delivery from a shell
This POSIX shell recipe uses OpenSSL and preserves the exact body bytes. Set
in the sender environment to the same secret as the server, and disable shell tracing when handling secrets. Do not put the secret value in command history.

body='{"order":{"id":"order-123"}}'
delivery_id='order-123@1'
timestamp=$(date +%s)
key_hex=$(printf '%s' "${ORDER_SIGNING_SECRET#whsec_}" | openssl base64 -d -A | od -An -v -tx1 | tr -d ' \n')
signature=$(printf '%s' "$delivery_id.$timestamp.$body" | openssl dgst -sha256 -mac HMAC -macopt "hexkey:$key_hex" -binary | openssl base64 -A)
unset key_hex
curl --fail-with-body 'https://your-archon-host/webhooks/sources/orders-production' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H "webhook-id: $delivery_id" \
  -H "webhook-timestamp: $timestamp" \
  -H "webhook-signature: v1,$signature" \
  --data-binary "$body"

cannot represent arbitrary binary keys. OpenSSL receives the key in its process arguments, so run this recipe on a trusted sender host. Send fresh timestamps when retrying, but retain the delivery ID and exact body. Timestamps must be within 300 seconds of receipt, in either direction. During key rotation the signature header can contain space-separated
entries; any matching entry authenticates the delivery.

is the durable dedup key within this source instance. A retry of a valid JSON delivery with the same ID and exact body returns 200 and creates no new receipt or start, even if a binding's run-as user has since been removed. Reusing the ID with different body bytes returns 409, even if the JSON values are equivalent. Binding edits do not change an already accepted delivery.

text.insert: A valid signature proves possession of the sender's key and integrity of the delivery. It does not make customer text or other event content trustworthy. Mapped inputs reach workflow prompts and scripts as untrusted data; author workflows accordingly. Map only the fields the workflow needs. Resolved inputs are persisted with the receipt's binding, including the whole body if you use
, and there is no automatic retention policy. Never map credentials into inputs.

Operator configuration owns the workflow, cwd, isolation, execution host, resource, and run-as user. The body can only supply configured input values, which preparation checks against the workflow's declarations; a workflow that declares no inputs receives none. It cannot choose any launch authority. The plugin reads secrets from the environment and never logs secrets, bodies, or signature headers. The signature covers the exact received bytes, including a leading byte-order mark. Authentication completes before receipt persistence.
Poll a system that cannot send webhooks

The host scheduler (cron, a systemd timer, launchd, or Task Scheduler) runs an operator-owned poll script. The script lists recent items and reports each with a stable delivery key made from its ID and version, encoded as a base64 JSON pair

in these recipes. Archon deduplicates within the configured source instance and admits the work. It keeps no poll cursor, runs no resident poller, and promises no catch-up. Choose the API's lookback window to cover scheduler downtime; items outside that window are the script's responsibility.
returns a JSON array of objects with string
fields. Each version must identify immutable content. Report a new version when an item changes, and keep the same key and input content across retries.

name: process-order
description: Record an order reported by a poll script.
mutates_checkout: false
inputs:
  order_id: { type: string, required: true }
nodes:
  - id: record
    bash: printf '%s\n' "$INPUTS_ORDER_ID" > "$ARTIFACTS_DIR/order.txt"
Replace the recording node with your order handling. Event values remain untrusted and are persisted with the receipt; pass only the fields the workflow needs.

containing the tools your workflows run for the scheduled user, and use absolute executable paths:

#!/bin/sh
set -eu
poll_dir=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$poll_dir"' EXIT HUP INT TERM
curl --fail --silent --show-error "$ORDERS_URL" > "$poll_dir/response.json"
jq -c '.[]' "$poll_dir/response.json" > "$poll_dir/items.jsonl"
while IFS= read -r item; do
  delivery_id=$(printf '%s' "$item" | jq -er '[.id, .version] | @base64')
  printf '%s' "$item" | jq -cS '{order_id: .id}' > "$poll_dir/inputs.json"
  /opt/archon/bin/archon trigger fire --config /srv/archon/polled-orders.json \
    --delivery-id "$delivery_id" --inputs "$poll_dir/inputs.json"
done < "$poll_dir/items.jsonl"
/opt/archon/bin/archon trigger drain --host orders-host
The final drain also advances queued work on ticks with no items. On CLI-only hosts, continue scheduling drains until queued work has started.

poll_dir=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$poll_dir"' EXIT HUP INT TERM
curl --fail --silent --show-error "$ORDERS_URL" > "$poll_dir/response.json"
jq -c '.[]' "$poll_dir/response.json" > "$poll_dir/items.jsonl"
while IFS= read -r item; do
  delivery_id=$(printf '%s' "$item" | jq -er '[.id, .version] | @base64')
  body=$(printf '%s' "$item" | jq -cS '{order: {id: .id}}')
  timestamp=$(date +%s)
  key_hex=$(printf '%s' "${ORDER_SIGNING_SECRET#whsec_}" | openssl base64 -d -A | od -An -v -tx1 | tr -d ' \n')
  signature=$(printf '%s' "$delivery_id.$timestamp.$body" | openssl dgst -sha256 -mac HMAC -macopt "hexkey:$key_hex" -binary | openssl base64 -A)
  unset key_hex
  curl --fail-with-body --silent --show-error "$ARCHON_WEBHOOK_URL" \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -H "webhook-id: $delivery_id" \
    -H "webhook-timestamp: $timestamp" \
    -H "webhook-signature: v1,$signature" \
    --data-binary "$body"
done < "$poll_dir/items.jsonl"
